turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. Well, my husband wanted me to come. I’m here because for nearly two years now, I’ve been absolutely sure the contractor and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They’re keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. 

And it’s such a shame because I picked out this lovely pale yellow paint for the walls. 'Morning Butter,' the little paper swatch said. It reminded me of my grandmother's kitchen back in Peoria. She used to bake these incredible rhubarb pies... oh, I haven't thought about her rhubarb in ages. The grocery store down the street never has the fresh kind anymore, just those frozen bags, and it's just not the same for baking. The crust gets all soggy. 

But anyway, no matter how many receipts my husband shows me—he keeps pulling them out of this ugly old shoebox he insists on using as a filing cabinet—or how many excuses the contractor and those people give me, I know what they're doing. They're all in it together to cheat us. Have you ever tried to find matching terracotta tiles, by the way? It's practically impossible since the hardware store on 5th street closed down last spring.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that her contractor and neighbors are conspiring to cheat her, which she maintains despite contradictory evidence like receipts.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from her core complaint to unrelated topics like paint colors, her grandmother's rhubarb pies, grocery stores, and terracotta tiles.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people do not?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Oh, no. No, I don't hear anything that isn't there, or see things either. My hearing and vision are sharp as a tack. Honestly, I wish my husband could say the same. He always has the television turned up so loud in the evenings. We watch Jeopardy! every night after dinner—Alex Trebek, God rest his soul, I still miss him. The new hosts just don't have that same charm, do they? 

But anyway, my husband blasts the volume so high it practically rattles the good china in the dining room hutch. I bought that hutch at an estate sale over on Elm Street... oh, it must have been thirty years ago now. The woman who owned it had the most beautiful collection of ceramic thimbles displayed in it. I've never seen anything like it, little hand-painted ones from all over Europe. I always meant to start a collection like that myself, but you know how time just gets away from you. 

But no, I don't hear voices or anything silly like that. Just the television being entirely too loud.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or seeing things that are not there.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually full of energy or needed much less sleep than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Full of energy? Oh, no, definitely not. I’ve always needed my full eight hours of sleep, maybe even nine these days. Although, getting a good night's rest has been so difficult lately because of that new mattress my husband insisted we buy. 

It’s one of those memory foam things, you know? The salesman at the store said it’s supposed to cradle your spine, but honestly, it just feels like sinking into a pit of warm mud. It actually reminds me of this spa treatment my sister convinced me to try when we went down to Sedona for her fiftieth birthday. They wrap you up in this heavy red clay... supposedly it draws out all your toxins, but I just felt like a giant baked potato. My sister, though, she loved it. She's always trying those new age health fads. Just last month she bought a machine that's supposed to make your drinking water alkaline. I told her regular tap water was perfectly fine for our parents, but she never listens. She even buys special Himalayan pink salt for her cooking now. 

But what were we talking about? Oh, right, energy. No, I don't get bursts of energy or stay up all night or anything like that. Just regular, everyday tiredness, especially when I can't get comfortable on that awful foam mattress.

symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having periods of being unusually full of energy or getting bursts of energy.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient denies needing less sleep, stating she has always needed her full eight or nine hours and does not stay up all night.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period of several days or longer when your mood was unusually high, irritable, or expansive?
turns.patient_response:
Unusually high? Oh, no. I'm a pretty even-keeled person, really. I don't get these big bursts of being overly happy or anything like that. And irritable... well, no more than anyone else, I suppose. I mean, I do get a little annoyed sometimes, like last Tuesday when I tried to call the cable company. The picture on our television has been getting all fuzzy right around four o'clock every afternoon. It’s the strangest thing. 

So I called them, and I was on hold for nearly forty-five minutes. They play that awful elevator music while you wait, you know the kind? It sounds like it's being played on a cheap synthesizer. My nephew Tommy used to have one of those little electronic keyboards when he was a boy. He drove my sister absolutely up the wall playing 'Chopsticks' over and over again. He’s a dentist now, over in Grand Rapids. Beautiful office he has, right near the river. He has three little girls of his own now, too. I sent them the cutest matching Easter dresses last spring, pale pink with little white daisies embroidered along the hem... 

But what was I saying? Oh, right, my mood. No, it's just normal. I don't get unusually high or angry or anything like that. Just the regular amount of frustration with things like the cable company.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering from a story about the cable company to elevator music, her nephew's childhood keyboard, his dental practice, and his daughters' dresses before losing her train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies experiencing periods of unusually high, overly happy, or irritable moods.

turns.doctor_question: During this time, have you had periods when you felt unusually depressed?
turns.patient_response:
Depressed? Oh, heavens no. I don't really have time to sit around feeling sad. I like to keep my hands busy, you know? Just yesterday I was out in the front yard trying to save my hydrangeas. The soil here is just so acidic, they always turn that bright blue color, but I really prefer the pink ones. My mother used to grow the most massive pink hydrangeas back in Ohio. 

We had this big wrap-around porch, and she’d cut them and put them in these heavy glass pitchers. She actually won a blue ribbon at the county fair for her floral arrangements in 1978. Or was it '79? It was the same year my brother bought that awful mustard-colored station wagon. The wood paneling on the side started peeling off after barely a year! He drove that thing all the way to Florida for a family vacation, and the air conditioning gave out somewhere in Georgia. We had to roll all the windows down, and the humidity just completely ruined my hair. I've always had naturally curly hair, you see, and the moment there's a drop of moisture in the air, it just frizzes right up like a poodle. I have to use this special serum I order from a catalog now just to keep it tame... 

But anyway, no, I don't get depressed. I just keep myself busy with my plants and things around the house.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from the topic of depression to hydrangeas, a station wagon, and hair frizz.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling depressed or sad, stating 'Depressed? Oh, heavens no.'
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient mentions keeping busy with her plants and activities around the house, indicating she has not lost interest in her hobbies.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been any times when those beliefs were present only when you were also having mood symptoms, like depression or feeling unusually energized?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. The things I know are happening... they're just happening all the time, regardless of my mood. It doesn't matter if I'm having a good day or a bad day. Like last Thursday, I was having a perfectly lovely morning. I had just finished baking a batch of my grandmother's oatmeal raisin cookies. 

She used to soak the raisins in warm water for ten minutes before mixing them into the dough, it makes them so plump and juicy. She learned that trick from a baker she met when she and my grandfather took a trip to Nova Scotia back in the early sixties. They brought back this beautiful hand-carved wooden seagull from that trip. It sat on the mantle in their living room for thirty years until my cousin knocked it over with a tennis racket. He was always a clumsy boy, that one. Broke his arm twice before he was ten just falling out of the same oak tree in their backyard. The second time, he actually had to have pins put in... 

But, oh, what were you asking? Right, the moods and the... the things I know. No, they aren't connected at all. I don't get depressed or overly energized, and the things I'm dealing with are just there, every single day.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off into a long, unrelated story about cookies, a trip to Nova Scotia, and a cousin's broken arm before losing track of the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly states, 'I don't get depressed.'
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies experiencing elevated mood, stating they do not get 'overly energized.'

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed that your thoughts or speech become hard for other people to follow?
turns.patient_response:
Hard for people to follow? Oh, I don't think so. I speak perfectly clearly. I've always prided myself on my enunciation. My high school English teacher, Mrs. Gable, used to say I had the most articulate reading voice in the entire class. We read 'To Kill a Mockingbird' out loud that year, and she always had me read the parts for Scout. 

Mrs. Gable was such a wonderful woman, she wore these beautiful silk scarves every single day, no matter the season. She had this one that was a deep emerald green with little gold paisley prints on it. I tried to find one just like it years later at a department store downtown, but the material just felt so cheap, you know? Like that synthetic polyester that makes you sweat the minute you put it on. I can't stand clothes that don't let your skin breathe. My neighbor, Betty, she wears these awful polyester tracksuits when she walks her dog. It's a little Pomeranian, yaps at absolutely everything that moves. The poor mailman practically has to sneak up to her porch just to drop off the letters... 

But no, nobody has ever told me I'm hard to understand. I just talk like I always have.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies that their speech is hard to follow, stating they speak perfectly clearly and nobody has ever told them they are hard to understand.
